Maladaptive Strategies.value: I push myself to exercise excessively

Negative Appraisals.value: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power
I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me
Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore

issues.item: Avoid Perpetrator Cues: Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me
issues.explanation: The trauma type is trauma to a loved one, but this maladaptive strategy presumes a direct perpetrator who harmed the patient. That is hard to reconcile unless the loved one's trauma also directly involved interpersonal harm to the patient, which is not indicated here.

issues.item: Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened
issues.explanation: Permanent humiliation is more characteristic of direct interpersonal victimization. With a loved-one trauma, this appraisal is not impossible, but in combination with 'others can see what happened to me' it implies a self-referential shame exposure theme that fits poorly unless the patient was also directly victimized.

vignette: The collapse of her younger brother's breathing in the emergency department left Aroha with a mind that could not unlearn the geometry of that room. She remembered the exact contour of the ICU waiting area, the way the narrow corridors forced her into a confined aisle, and the relentless antiseptic sting that clung to her coat long after they wheeled him away. When the staff began speaking in overlapping, technical cadences that dissolved into incomprehensible chatter, she felt the floor tilt beneath her. Those three sensations-the confining physical space, the sterile chemical scent, the garbled vocal rush-became her first warning system. Whenever Aroha now walked past a clinic entrance or caught that same chemical tang in a newly finished architectural model, her pulse spiked, and the old terror that she would lose him all over again rushed back. Those unavoidable spatial cues and chemical odors did more than spark panic; they fundamentally altered how she viewed herself. She was certain that her vulnerability was stamped across her face, that others could see exactly what had happened to her. She had come to believe the world was hostile, that her faith in people and any higher power had evaporated, leaving her with a hollow conviction that nothing she designed or achieved could ever hold meaning again. Aroha's responses solidified over the following months. The moment she recognized those spatial boundaries or caught the hospital smell drifting from a colleague's hand sanitizer at her firm, she immediately retreated. She stopped answering phone calls, telling friends she was overwhelmed when she was actually locking her studio door. She began pushing herself through grueling, solitary runs until her muscles trembled, and she avoided all medical cues, swerving her car at ambulance sirens and cancelling every routine physical exam. These compulsive workouts and social withdrawals offered temporary relief, yet they quickly bred the very fears they were meant to silence. Isolating from her friends and exhausting her body convinced her that she was fundamentally broken and utterly alone, which only deepened her conviction that she was exposed to others' judgment. Pushing through endless laps and dodging social ties also kept her hyper-vigilant; her physical exhaustion lowered her threshold for stress, making every unfamiliar location and muffled conversation feel immediately threatening. Her internal landscape continued to feed the cycle. Believing she had lost all faith and that life held no meaning, Aroha stopped looking for safety and instead scanned every environment for proof of her doom. This hopeless expectation amplified her sensory alertness; when she walked into a client presentation in a glass-walled medical building, the sheer size of the open plan and the murmur of overlapping conversations triggered a panic so acute it mirrored the hospital corridor. What frightened her most was that her own avoidance had become a mirror reflecting her worst fears back at her. Because she was convinced she could not be trusted or understood, she doubled down on her withdrawal. She interpreted her own anxiety as a personal failing, which only justified her further retreat from friends and her escalation into compulsive exercise. She told herself she had no choice but to stay apart, to keep moving until the thoughts quieted, never realizing that her flight from connection and her rigid routines were the very engines keeping her terror alive. It was the day she stood paralyzed in the middle of her drafting table, unable to complete a single line for a hospital wing project, that she finally called a therapist. She had spent years drafting structures meant to shelter families, yet she could not build a single safe place for herself. She wanted the panic to stop, but she was terrified that seeking help would force her back into the very rooms, smells, and sounds that had already taught her the world was unsafe.
